title: Toward continuous shrinkage measurement of poured earth: practical setup and underlying shrinking mechanisms
abstract: Abstract Continuous shrinkage measurement in earth-based materials remains technically challenging, particularly for high-water-content mixtures with low initial stiffness. In this study, a semi-cylindrical experimental setup, combined with digital image correlation (DIC) for measurements of surface strains and a linear variable differential transformer (LVDT) for interior strains, is proposed and validated to track the shrinkage behavior of pourable earth materials. Mass loss, surface temperature, and capillary pressure were simultaneously measured and compared with those of conventional prismatic specimens. Both geometries exhibit comparable drying kinetics under identical environmental conditions, with an initial constant-rate period (CRP) followed by a falling-rate period (FRP). However, the semi-cylindrical geometry yields a shorter CRP and enhanced moisture uniformity across the drying depth, attributed to a higher surface-to-volume ratio. During the CRP, shrinkage increased linearly with the volume of evaporated water. In the FRP, shrinkage in both geometries followed the Biot–Bishop effective-stress framework. Although some degree of differential shrinkage remained within the semi-cylindrical specimen, the deformation measured in the interior corresponded more closely to macroscopic water loss, demonstrating that LVDT measurements allow tracking in a simple and practical manner the bulk shrinkage behavior during drying.

sections.heading: Introduction
paragraphs: Widely available, recyclable earth materials are experiencing a renaissance in the construction sector, due to their low environmental footprints and excellent hygrothermal properties [ 1 ]. The reuse of excavation materials that would be otherwise landfilled facilitates the decarbonization of embodied and operational carbon footprints in the construction industry [ 2 3 ]. Earth construction has a long history in human civilization; diverse construction techniques, such as rammed earth, cob, and adobe, have been utilized since millennia to build both simple dwellings and representative architecture [ 4 ]. To engineer this material to catch up with the contemporary construction pace and fashion, construction efficiency, mechanical strength, and durability need to be improved. Indeed, recent progress included different aspects as processing [ 5 ,  6 ,  7 ,  8 – 9 ], e.g., 3D printing [ 10 ] and self-flowable earth [ 11 ], prefabrication [ 12 ], with increased automation, and environmentally friendly stabilization [ 13 ]. In particular, poured earth is liquefied using clay dispersants, which enable casting like regular concrete, also with a reduced water content. After pouring, the materials coagulate or set to allow early demolding within 1–2 days [ 9 14 ]. Poured earth holds considerable potential for scaling up the use of earth-based materials, as it can utilize the existing facilities of the concrete sector, thereby obviating the need for additional investments. Besides, the pourable characteristics ease the time- and labor-intensive drawbacks of earthen construction, which is especially important when applying earth materials in backfilling or monolithic cast walls, which require pumping and casting.

Recent research efforts have focused on expanding the mix design choices [ 11 15 ,  16 ,  17 – 18 ], improving the water resistance [ 19 ], and addressing the variability of the soil [ 20 21 ]. Due to its high water content and moderate stiffness, shrinkage induced by drying [ 22 ] is very pronounced in poured earth, being several times larger than in rammed earth or earth bricks and even orders of magnitude larger than in concrete [ 23 ]. In the worst case, it can lead to cracking, potentially jeopardizing the long-term structural integrity and limiting its practical applications. Shrinkage and cracking of clay or soil have been extensively studied by researchers in the field of geotechnics and earth sciences [ 24 ,  25 ,  26 – 27 ]. The soil shrinkage characteristic curve, i.e., the void volume change along with the water loss, can be characterized by the shrinkage limit, linear shrinkage tests, or advanced methods such as image analysis [ 28 ] or digital image correlation (DIC) [ 29 ]. By correlating the measured shrinkage with the water content evolution, determined by measuring the mass of specimens at regular time intervals, different phases of volume changes during the drying process can be detected, which helps to identify the underlying mechanisms. When exposed to drying, soil evaporation will undergo three stages: the constant rate period (CRP), where the water is lost at a constant rate, followed by falling rate period I and II (FRP I, II), during which the rate of water loss diminishes progressively [ 30 ]. An illustrative diagram for elucidating the different stages can be found in [ 31 ]. Specifically, the constant evaporation rate in the CRP is sustained by menisci formed at the drying surface, which act as capillary pumps that bring water from the interior of the soil to the surface [ 32 ]. The CRP persists as long as the capillary paths between the drying surface and the interior remain connected. Once the menisci retreat from the surface, the evaporation rate begins to fall, and a new drying front starts forming at a certain depth within the material [ 31 ]. In this new stage (FRP I), water is driven both by capillary flow (in the underlying wet region) and vapor diffusion (in the air-dry areas) [ 33 ]. With growing thickness of the dry surface layer, the evaporation rate is further reduced, and the system enters FRP II, where water loss is mainly governed by vapor diffusion [ 31 ]. It has been reported that the reduction in water volume corresponds to a 1:1 linear decrease in bulk volume during the CRP, considering the absence of pressure gradients [ 34 35 ]. The capillary pressure developed within the pore network after the air entry in the FRP stages plays a major contribution to the shrinkage-induced stress and cracking [ 36 37 ]. Simultaneously, water content gradients caused by non-uniform drying often lead to differential strains and thus internal stress; this issue is particularly serious when using earth to bear loads in buildings, since it inevitably requires structural members of considerable thickness because of its low strength [ 38 ].

When measuring the shrinkage of soil as a building material, standard methods such as length change of specimens of different sizes and shapes are commonly employed [ 10 39 ,  40 ,  41 ,  42 – 43 ], which, however, fail to capture the full deformation profile. To the knowledge of the authors, only very few methods are able to measure the shrinkage of earth materials from wet consistency to totally dried conditions [ 44 ]. Measuring the shrinkage of poured earth with methods based on length-change is problematic, particularly for the mixtures that do not incorporate hydraulic binders. The latter cannot achieve sufficient strength and stiffness for demolding unless they have dried to a certain extent. Yet, most of the shrinkage occurs exactly during this period. Therefore, it is paramount to develop measurement methods that can continuously track the deformation of poured earth from casting and during the whole drying process. The mitigation of shrinkage and cracking of earth-based materials, to date, has predominantly been tackled by conventional methods, including stabilization with hydraulic binders [ 45 ] and the incorporation of natural and synthetic fibers [ 46 47 ]. While stabilization effectively reduces shrinkage and fibers can limit crack widths, there is a lack of systematic understanding of the mechanisms by which these additives influence different stages of shrinkage. Uncovering the underlying mechanisms is therefore crucial for developing more rational shrinkage mitigation solutions and implementing effective measures when shrinkage cracking is most severe.

Useful insights for shrinkage measurements of earth-based materials can be drawn from studies on early-age deformations of cement-based materials, where researchers have employed a variety of contact and non-contact measurement techniques from casting through to the hardened stage. Those techniques include digital image correlation (DIC) [ 48 ,  49 ,  50 – 51 ], linear variable differential transformers (LVDTs) with [ 52 ] or without corrugated tubes [ 53 ], laser sensors [ 54 ], X-ray computed tomography (CT) [ 55 ] and rheology measurements [ 56 ]. Extensive studies regarding the measurement conditions, shrinkage mechanisms, and additives for shrinkage control have been conducted on cement-based materials.

The present study aims to design a practical and precise experimental setup capable of continuously tracking the shrinkage behavior of poured earth during drying. The setup is intended to identify the various shrinkage stages, enabling the provision of fundamental mechanistic studies for the shrinkage behavior of poured earth. In fact, the shrinkage studies reported in the literature predominantly focus on small specimens (typically prisms with cubic cross sections ranging from 25 to 40 mm), which do not anticipate the cracking risks arising from the moisture and shrinkage gradient often present in larger specimens. In this study, a large-sized semi-cylindrical mould, to simulate the real-case moisture gradient and meanwhile minimize the geometry restriction, was designed to test the deformation of earth specimens during drying using LVDT sensors and DIC. For comparison, the shrinkage measurements were also conducted on prismatic specimens using DIC. Mass change, surface temperature evolution, and capillary pressure build-up were investigated as well to correlate the measured shrinkage with the different stages of drying.

sections.heading: Materials and specimen preparation
paragraphs: Sandy clay (Lehm-Mauermörtel Schwer by Claytec, hereinafter referred to as LMS), but amended with 10 mass-% illite-rich clay (hereinafter referred to as IL_R) to increase the clay fractions to make the mixture more suitable for pouring, was used. The mineralogical composition estimated by a combination of Rietveld quantification from the XRD, XRF, and TGA data is displayed in Table  1 . The particle size distribution of the two clays, measured using a laser particle size analyzer (PSA, Anton Paar) in isopropanol dispersion, is displayed in Fig.  1 . After amending, the cation exchange capacity (CEC), measured by cobalt hexamine trichloride exchange as detailed in [ 57 ] of the mixture is 5 ± 1 meq/100 g, with a specific density of 2.65 g/cm 3  (He-pycnometry). Table 1 Mineralogical composition of the two utilized earth materials, with errors evaluated to 15 and 10% of the given values for clay minerals and the rest, respectively Phase, mass% Clay mineral Quartz Dolomite Calcite Microcline Muscovite Kaolinite Smectite Illite LMS – 4 7 85 4 – – – IL_R 14 3 36 26 – 4 5 12 Fig. 1 Particle size distribution of the tested IL_R and LMS materials

Specimen preparation was conducted in a room with controlled temperature (20 ± 2 °C) and relative humidity (70 ± 5% RH). 8 kg of the dry mixture were manually homogenized in the mixing bowl before adding water. A water-to-clay ratio of 0.1714 that allows the achievement of a 150 mm spread in the mini slump test [ 58 ] was chosen. Following the dry mixing, water was slowly added to the mixture, and the entire mixture was mixed for 3 min at slow speed using a Planetary Hobart mortar mixer. A break was then taken to remove materials adhering to the bowl wall, after which the mixture was mixed for a further 3 min. Subsequently, the wet mixture was cast into the moulds and sealed with plastic film. Specimens were then preconditioned in a shrinkage measurement room at 35 ± 1 °C and 38 ± 8% RH for 2 h to minimize the thermal expansion, due to the lower mixing temperature but higher testing temperature, of specimens at an early age [ 50 ]. In the following, without special mention, time zero refers to the start time of measurement after the preconditioning period.

sections.heading: Measurement setup and conditions
paragraphs: The experimental program comprises shrinkage measurements on prismatic and semi-cylindrical specimens under accelerated one-sided drying. Deformation, mass loss, surface temperature, and capillary pressure were monitored, while the water-retention curve was determined separately. The capillary-pressure and retention data were subsequently used to support the interpretation of the drying-induced shrinkage.

Prismatic moulds with a square upper face, commonly used for measuring the free shrinkage of cementitious mortar [ 51 ], with dimensions of 50 × 250 × 250 mm 3 , were initially used for shrinkage measurements using the DIC technique. Additionally, a semi-cylindrical mould with an inner diameter of 85 mm, a depth of 50 mm, and a length of 300 mm was employed. The geometry scheme and mould setup are illustrated in Fig.  2 . This geometry was chosen to limit sharp corners, where retained liquid film may cause local variations in moisture transport and differential shrinkage [ 59 ]. In addition, the corner region might be poorly compacted and present large pores. These effects may generate tensile stress and increase the risk of crack initiation. Besides, in a thin slab geometry, the earth specimen could curl and crack due to shrinkage gradients in depth. Two LVDT sensors, affixed to screws with lengths of 40 mm and diameters of 8 mm, were placed on two sides of the mould. A steel ring was mounted to the screw, acting as an anchor to increase the bonding between the screws and the earth materials, and it was embedded 18 mm into the mixture. The sensors were positioned 20 mm deep from the surface of the specimens. Fig. 2 Semi-cylindrical moulds used for measurements of the shrinkage of earth materials

An accelerated drying condition according to ASTM C1579-13 [ 60 ] for assessing the plastic shrinkage cracking of cementitious materials was adopted to speed up the drying process. It should be noted that the deformation of earth materials upon drying varies with the drying conditions. While accelerated drying conditions generally do not represent the actual shrinkage behavior of poured earth in practice, the correlation between water evaporation and deformation observed in these experiments remains generally valid [ 61 ]. The tests were conducted in a climate chamber with a controlled temperature of 35 ± 1 °C and humidity of 38 ± 8% RH. Additionally, wind with a speed of 7.5 ± 0.5 m/s, generated by an air blower, was blown over the surface of specimens to increase the drying speed. The aforementioned conditions were realized with a dedicated setup extensively used for cementitious materials; the setup is presented in Fig.  3 a, while further details can be found in the literature [ 49 50 ]. Fig. 3 a  Setup used for measurements of shrinkage of earth materials, together with the  b ,  c  measured specimens, where LVDT sensors were embedded inside the specimen, and the  d  DIC identifiers were placed on the top of the specimens for tracking the deformation, respectively

sections.heading: Shrinkage measurement
paragraphs: Before the measurements, the LVDT sensors were calibrated using a micrometer with known displacements. A digital data acquisition system recorded displacement at a frequency of 1 Hz, with each measurement representing the average of 100 readings per second from the LVDT. DIC measurements were performed following the method developed by Ghourchian et al. [ 48 49 ], wherein light metal wire meshes with black and white patterns on their upper face were placed onto the surface of the specimen (Fig.  3 b, c), acting as targets to track the deformations (see Fig.  3 d). The mass and the geometry of the wire meshes are designed to prevent both sinking into the fresh mixture and being blown away by the wind. Additionally, the mesh does not affect air flow at the surface or water evaporation from surfaces. Three meshes were placed on each semi-cylindrical specimen, while five meshes were used for the prismatic specimens. At defined time intervals, images were captured by two correlated cameras, and in-plane and out-of-plane deformation was evaluated by analyzing the displacements of the aforementioned black-and-white patterns in a subset of pixels between captured images using Istra 4D software. It should be noted that only DIC measurements were used for prismatic specimens, whereas both DIC and LVDTs were used for semi-cylindrical specimens.

sections.heading: Surface temperature, mass loss, and capillary pressure
paragraphs: The drying was limited to 1D, 1-sided moisture flow for specimens of both geometries, i.e., only the top surface of the specimens was exposed, with the sides or the curved surface and the base sealed with plastic film foil to prevent evaporation and reduce adhesion between specimen and formwork. This configuration ensured that moisture gradients developed solely along the vertical axis. The drying experiment was carried out for 60 h. The surface temperature of the specimens was monitored with a thermal imaging camera. A series of images was captured at 1-min intervals, and the temperature field was analyzed using IRSoft software. A balance with a maximum load of 60 kg and an accuracy of 0.001 kg logged the mass of the specimens (around 15 kg with moulds) during the drying process at 1 min intervals. Two specimens per mixture were cast when a prismatic mold was employed, while three specimens were cast when a semi-cylindrical mold was employed. The capillary pressure during drying was monitored with tensiometers (TEROS 31, METER). Three sensors, with a diameter of 5 mm and accuracy of ± 0.15 kPa, were embedded at depths of 5, 25, and 45 mm beneath the exposed drying surface to monitor the capillary pressure profile over time. The prismatic specimen was the same size as that for the shrinkage measurements, whereas the semi-cylindrical specimen was reduced to 185 mm in length with the same diameter.

sections.heading: Water retention curve
Drying kinetics in specimens of different geometries
Surface temperature
paragraphs: The temperature evolution of earth materials is intricately linked to the stages of evaporation and to the evaporation rate, and indeed can be utilized to differentiate these stages [ 30 ]. Figure  5  illustrates the surface temperature of the prismatic and semicylindrical earth specimens, as measured by the thermal camera, together with the ambient temperature. For both specimens (which were preconditioned at 35 °C for 2 h), upon drying, the surface temperature decreased abruptly, followed by a period of approximately 25 °C, i.e., 10°K lower than the ambient temperature. It should be noted that the initial temperature did not reach 35 °C but reached 30 °C, because the 2 h precondition is not enough to equilibrate the temperature. The constant period at 25 °C following the initial rapid decrease corresponds to the constant rate period (CRP), during which the surface temperature is governed by the balance between heat exchange with the surrounding air and endothermic evaporative cooling of water. Subsequently, the temperature of the surface gradually increased to equilibrate with the ambient temperature, indicating that the FRP stage had begun, during which the rate of water loss diminished progressively. Note that the CRP period is shorter for the cylindrical specimen compared to the prismatic specimen, with around 3.5–4 h compared to 5.5–6 h. Besides, the temperature of the prismatic specimen rose at a slower rate than that of the cylindrical specimen, indicating that the same earth materials cast in the prismatic moulds dry more slowly than those in cylindrical moulds. The differences are due to the ratio of exposed surface area to specimen volume: the prismatic specimen exhibits a lower ratio of 0.02 mm⁻ 1  than the semi-cylindrical specimens (about 0.03 mm −1 ), which facilitates drying. Fig. 5 Temperature evolution of earth specimens prepared in different geometries with inserted zoomed view of first 5 h. The ambient temperature of the room was also monitored at the same time as each specimen measurement, marked in red, using the same method for comparison

sections.heading: Water loss
paragraphs: Figure  6  presents the cumulative mass change of earth specimens with different geometries after conditioning for 2 h in the climatic chamber. Pure water used for casting, with and without preconditioning for 2 h at 35 °C before testing, was also measured. Upon evaporation, pure water exhibits a constant linear mass loss, with a rate of approximately 0.75 and 1.1 kg m −2  h −1 , respectively, for non-preconditioned and preconditioned conditions. The two earth specimens exhibit similar trends in mass change, despite their different geometries. Specifically, the mass loss follows a linear decrease over time at the beginning, with an evaporation rate of around 1.0 kg m −2  h −1  over a duration of 5.5–6 h for prismatic specimens and of a rate of approximately 1.05 kg m −2  h −1  over the initial 4–5 h for semi-cylindrical specimens. Though also experimental scatter may play a role, the slightly higher evaporation rate may be attributed to the higher surface temperature of the cylindrical specimens (Fig.  5 ). At the given drying conditions and specimen mixture, the initial water evaporation rate from a wet surface is solely related to the surface temperature of the specimen, as shown previously with the higher evaporation rate of water at higher temperature [ 65 ]. During the 2 h of preconditioning in the chamber before the experiment, the temperature of the semi-cylindrical specimen, due to its lower surface-to-volume ratio, came closer to temperature equilibrium than that of the prismatic specimen. Consequently, the cylindrical specimen displays a slightly higher initial water loss rate compared to the prismatic specimens, but similar to the evaporation rate of pure water. The semi-cylindrical specimen also exhibits a faster decrease in the average gravimetric water content over drying time compared to the prismatic specimen (see supporting information, Fig.  S1 , with detailed values listed in Table  S1 ). The drying kinetics of unconditioned rectangular earth specimens with thicknesses of 28, 34, and 50 mm, as illustrated in Fig. S2, indicate that all specimens displayed a comparable mass loss rate, similar to that of pure water, during the CRP, further supporting the above finding. The duration of the CRP corresponds well with the temperature plateau shown in Fig.  5 . The shorter CRP of the semi-cylindrical specimen is due to its higher exposed surface area to volume ratio in comparison to the prismatic specimen, consequently resulting in an earlier onset of the falling rate period (this is shown very clearly also in Fig. S2). Fig. 6 Mass loss of earth specimens with different geometries and of pure water specimens over drying time

sections.heading: Capillary pressure
paragraphs: The evolution of matric potential (capillary pressure) at different depths within semi-cylindrical and prismatic specimens is presented in Fig.  7 . During the drying process, distinct capillary pressure gradients developed in both specimen geometries, as evidenced by the depth-dependent variation in matric potential over time. Despite the mass loss exhibiting a linear trend at the early stage of drying (Fig.  6 ), the moisture loss of the soil was not uniform, with the surface drying more rapidly than the inner layer. A small positive pressure (due to the hydraulic head) was observed for all positions at the beginning, with deeper positions displaying a higher positive value. In the semi-cylindrical specimen, the matric potential at the near-surface position starts to fall approximately 0.3 h after evaporation begins and decreases most rapidly, reaching values below −160 kPa within approximately 6 h. It should be noted that the tensiometer can only measure the matric potential shortly after the air entry; beyond that, the measurement typically fails due to air penetration into the porous head of the tensiometer itself (refer to the endpoint of each curve). At greater depths (25 mm and 45 mm), the onset of capillary pressure is delayed by approximately 0.5 h and 2.7 h, respectively, relative to shallower locations. These deeper positions also demonstrate more gradual decreases and extended periods prior to air invasion. Notably, despite the global mass change curve indicating a constant-rate period during the initial hours of evaporation, capillary pressure begins to develop, and a moisture gradient along the depth profile forms. Although surface evaporation is sustained by internal water transport that supplies sufficient water to the surface, locally air entry and drying initiates, and a hydraulic gradient forms to maintain the evaporation flux within the macroscopically constant-rate regime. The prismatic specimen exhibited similar trends. The measuring position closest to the upper surface (5 mm depth) again showed the fastest drop in matric potential, falling below −150 kPa in under 7 h. At the middle depth (25 mm) and the bottom (45 mm), drying was slower. These results confirm that a vertical moisture gradient develops during evaporation, influenced by specimen geometry and depth, with surface layers drying faster and experiencing greater capillary pressure buildup. The data highlight the heterogeneous nature of drying and underscore the importance of depth-specific measurements for evaluating soil water dynamics and shrinkage deformation. Fig. 7 Evolution of the matric potential during the drying process at different depths in semi-cylindrical and prismatic specimens

By converting the measured capillary pressure through the corresponding water retention curve (Fig.  4 ), the saturation profile along the depth for the semi-cylindrical and prismatic specimens during the drying process can be calculated, as shown in Fig.  8 . In both geometries, the saturation decreases rapidly near the exposed surface and more gradually with depth, forming a clear drying front that migrates downward over time. Although both specimens begin fully saturated and display broadly similar evaporation rates (Fig.  6 ), their internal desaturation patterns differ. In the semi-cylindrical specimen, the saturation curves at 5 and 25 mm remain relatively close throughout the test, indicating that desaturation progresses at similar rates across the depth. This behavior reflects a more uniform drying pattern, with limited moisture gradients developing inside the specimen. In contrast, the prismatic specimen displays a pronounced separation between the saturation–depth curves: the surface zone desaturates early and rapidly, whereas the deeper measurements remain near saturation for a substantial period. This results in strong vertical moisture gradients and a highly non-uniform drying profile. Because both specimens share the same material composition, initial water content, and overall drying rate, the explanation for this behavior lies in the geometry. The semi-cylindrical shape exposes a higher effective drying surface per unit volume (as also observed in the earlier transition from CRP to FRP shown in Fig.  6 ). In contrast, the prismatic specimen, with a lower surface exposure per volume, retains moisture for longer at comparable depths, leading to a less uniform desaturation profile. These differences in internal moisture gradients are directly relevant to drying shrinkage: the semi-cylindrical specimen is expected to undergo more homogeneous deformation, while the prismatic specimen develops larger shrinkage gradients between the surface and the depth, which also induces self-induced stresses and could lead to cracking. Fig. 8 Saturation evaluation calculated based on capillary pressure and water retention curve, along the depth for the specimen's different geometries over drying time

sections.heading: Surface shrinkage and settlement measured with DIC
paragraphs: The shrinkage of earth materials is closely linked to water evaporation. In view of the observed difference in mass loss rate of earth specimens of two different geometries, vertical and horizontal shrinkage were plotted as functions of average gravimetric water content, rather than drying time, as shown in Figs.  9  and  10 . The line represents the average deformation, while the shaded regions in the figures indicate the standard deviation. Figure  9  illustrates the settlement in relation to water content, as measured by DIC on specimens of both geometries. The settlement calculated directly from the mass loss assumes that all water lost from the specimen directly results in settlement; this would be only valid if a) no horizontal deformation occurs and b) no internal empty porosity is formed when the water is lost, i.e., all water-filled pores collapse when they empty. Due to technical issues of the DIC, the measurements on semi-cylindrical specimens ended at a water content of 0.11 (corresponding to a mass loss of 5.7 kg/m 2 ). Analogous to the settlement behavior of fresh concrete, three distinct stages can be identified for both specimens: a linear stage, a transition stage, and a cessation stage. Within the linear stage, the measured settlement of the semi-cylindrical specimen is higher than that of the prismatic specimen, but lower than the theoretical bleeding settlement (see Fig. S3). In concrete, a good correlation between the settlement and the bleeding has been reported; in fact, the initial evaporation of water resulted in vertical deformation without significant horizontal shrinkage [ 48 ]. On the contrary, for the earth materials examined in this study, the evaporation of water resulted in simultaneous vertical and horizontal deformations. For prismatic and semi-cylindrical specimens, the linear stage begins to slow down approximately at a water content of 0.14 and 0.13; thereafter, a phase of expansion occurs for water contents around 0.135 and 0.125, followed by a plateau at water content around 0.125 and 0.115, respectively. Since the expansion occurs during the CRP stage of drying (Fig.  6 ), in which the temperature remains constant, temperature changes can be excluded as the cause. The time of reversal in vertical deformation corresponds well to the time when the matric suction of the bottom layer initiated; more specifically, it occurred beyond the air entry value (~ 3.3 h for the semicylindrical specimen, while ~ 3.6 h for the prismatic specimen, see Fig.  7 ). Besides, the point of vertical deformation arrest appears earlier than the end of the constant rate period, as identified in Fig.  5 . This unexpected trend might suggest the initiation of specimen curling due to the suction gradient, which will be discussed in detail in Sect. 3.2.2. Fig. 9 Vertical deformation measured on prismatic and semi-cylindrical specimens as a function of average gravimetric water content Fig. 10 Horizontal deformation measured on prismatic and semi-cylindrical specimens as a function of average water content

Figure  10  presents the horizontal deformation relative to average water content, measured on specimens of two different geometries. Regardless of geometry, earth specimens display similar deformation trends compared to vertical deformation. Within the margin of measurement error, the horizontal deformations were nearly identical until reaching a water content of 0.135, corresponding to a mass loss of approximately 4.0 kg/m 2 . Beyond this point, the shrinkage rate of the prismatic specimen declined and plateaued around a cumulative water content of 0.09. The shrinkage of the semi-cylindrical specimen continues at about the same slope until reaching a water content of around 0.12, with a mass loss of 4.5 kg/m 2 . Subsequently, the horizontal deformation continues to increase at a reduced rate. The transition points observed on the horizontal deformation curves align well with the reversal point in the vertical deformation graph (Fig.  9 ), which occurs earlier than the end of the CRP. Furthermore, the horizontal deformation measured on a semi-cylindrical specimen exceeds that of a prismatic specimen; the reasons will be explained later in Sect. 3.3.2.

sections.heading: Shrinkage deformation measured on semi-cylindrical specimen
paragraphs: The evolution of longitudinal shrinkage strain, as measured by DIC on the surface and LVDT in the middle of the specimen, over water content for the semi-cylindrical specimen is presented in Fig.  11 . Both curves exhibit typical shrinkage responses associated with moisture loss. However, there are distinct differences between the two curves. First, the LVDT-measured shrinkage shows a delayed response compared to surface measurements during the early stages of mass loss. Up to a water content of approximately 0.17 (corresponding to a mass loss of approximately 0.8 kg/m 2 ), the LVDTs did not detect any deformation, whereas DIC recorded a surface deformation of approximately 5000 μstrain. This might be due to a well-known artefact that also occurs in measurements of strain of cementitious materials at early ages [ 66 ], which will be discussed in Sect. 3.3.1. Additionally, the DIC measurement shows a steeper increase in shrinkage during the proportional stage than the LVDT, likely due to faster moisture evaporation and a steeper humidity gradient near the surface. In contrast, the strain in the middle layer increases gradually, lagging behind the surface response. Moreover, the middle layer exhibits a late transition to the residual shrinkage stage, indicating that the earth materials in the middle layer consolidated later than those at the surface. The final shrinkage strain reaches approximately 45,000 µstrain at the surface and 35,000 µstrain in the middle layer, supporting the presence of a differential deformation throughout the depth of the specimen. This non-uniform strain field across the thickness will create internal stress gradients that cause the specimen to curl toward the drying surface [ 67 ]. Prior to the AEV, the pores remain fully saturated, and the skeleton is relatively compliant, allowing the stress to dissipate with limited internal stress buildup. Once air entry occurs, especially in the bottom layer of the specimen, the capillary menisci and the resulting increased stiffness will accumulate notable interlayer stress [ 68 ], leading to more pronounced curling, which is the reason for the vertical expansion shown in Fig.  9 . Such internal tensile stress also may increase the potential for cracking or delamination (although no cracks were observed in this specific case) . Fig. 11 Longitudinal shrinkage measure on the surface by DIC and in the middle layer by LVDT on a semi-cylindrical earth specimen

sections.heading: Drying-induced shrinkage in the CRP
paragraphs: As expected, with the assumption of isotropic horizontal shrinkage, Eqs.  5  and  7  yield the same result.

During the initial drying phase, the computed volumetric shrinkage closely aligned with the total volume of evaporated water, in accordance with the anticipated proportional shrinkage behavior during the CRP. In the early phase of the CRP, the earth materials remain close to saturation, meaning that the volume reduction is primarily caused by pore collapse after water removal [ 25 69 ]. Therefore, during the early drying stage, the calculated volumetric shrinkage closely correlates with the cumulative volume of water evaporated. It should be noted that the volumetric shrinkage is calculated assuming uniform longitudinal shrinkage along the depth. Thus, the mismatch between LVDT and DIC results at an early age (Fig.  11 ) is primarily due to an instrumentation coupling issue: the LVDT likely failed to track very small, early distributed contractions of the soft material (local compliance or tip/slip effects).

As drying continues, the match between volumetric shrinkage and the volume of water evaporated no longer holds, and a clear deviation from the 1:1 relationship is observed, with volumetric shrinkage becoming smaller than the corresponding water loss. This detachment corresponds to the onset of expansion in the vertical direction (Fig.  9 ) and occurs earlier in the prismatic specimen than in the semi-cylindrical specimen, indicating more uniform shrinkage in the latter. During the CRP, a pronounced moisture gradient develops within the specimen, regardless of the geometry of the sample, with lower water contents near the exposed surfaces and higher water contents in the interior, accompanied by a suction gradient along the drying front (Fig.  7 ). As a result, the air-entry value (AEV) is first reached locally at the surface, while the interior remains saturated. Despite this partial desaturation, water flow from the interior sustains evaporation at a constant rate, allowing the macroscopic CRP to extend beyond the point of local air entry. With respect to shrinkage, once air entry occurs, part of the evaporated water contributes to pore emptying rather than volumetric contraction, leading to a deviation from proportional shrinkage. The detachment from the 1:1 line approximately corresponds to the stage when suction in the deeper layers approaches the AEV, at which point pore emptying becomes more pronounced throughout the specimen.

As for the reason why air enters the matrix, the evaporation rate remains unchanged. Based on the literature on the drying of homogeneous porous media, the transition from the CRP to FRP is associated with the loss of water continuity at the evaporating surface, which occurs when the matric suction reaches the air-entry value, and the pore water starts to evaporate, albeit at a reduced rate [ 70 ]. However, for earth materials of relatively large thickness, the air-entry condition is first reached locally near the exposed surfaces, while the interior remains at much lower suction. The resulting suction difference is sufficient to sustain the water flow toward the drying surface, with the pores at the drying front beginning to empty. As drying proceeds, the drying front moves downward, draining interstitial pore water. At the macroscopic scale, these two actions extend the CRP beyond the AEV. In synthesis, the shrinkage of earth materials with relatively high thickness in the CRP initially follows a transport-dominated pattern (proportional shrinkage) but later transitions to a stress-dominated pattern. Due to the more uniform drying in the semi-cylindrical specimen compared to the prismatic specimen, the aforementioned transition happened later as well.

sections.heading: Drying-induced shrinkage in the FRP
paragraphs: Without considering the self-induced stresses arising from the differential shrinkage between the surface and the interior layers, using the data presented in Fig.  13 , the elastic modulus can be calculated, and the results, as a function of saturation, are shown in Fig.  14 . In all specimens, the modulus increases markedly as saturation decreases, confirming a pronounced stiffening of the material during drying. The general trend is similar with different specimen geometries, with the computed elastic modulus varying from 100 kPa to 2 MPa within the calculated unsaturated range. These values align with the reported ranges for sandy and clayey soils [ 77 ] (also shown in Fig.  14 ), indicating the validity of the Biot-Bishop theory in calculating the shrinkage or elastic modulus for earth materials. The rapid increase in modulus at low saturation explains why the shrinkage rate slows down in the late stage of the FRP. When the stiffness becomes sufficiently high, further increases in suction-induced effective stress yield only a negligible incremental strain. Consequently, although moisture loss and suction may continue to evolve, the macroscopic shrinkage rate decreases dramatically; indeed, this is often called in the literature the "zero-shrinkage stage" [ 69 ] due to the very small shrinkage rate. Overall, despite differences in drying history across layers and geometries, the shrinkage behavior of earth materials in the FRP is consistent with an effective stress–modulus framework. Fig. 13 Longitudinal shrinkage of different specimens as a function of the calculated effective stress according to the Biot-Bishop theory Fig. 14 Calculated elastic modulus and associated fitted line based on the power function as a function of saturation degree

sections.heading: Practical implications
paragraphs: As previously discussed, semi-cylindrical specimens promote more uniform drying than prismatic geometries, producing smoother suction gradients across the cross-section. In contrast, prismatic specimens develop more pronounced moisture gradients between the surface and the interior. Given the low strength and stiffness of earth materials, a reduced suction gradient will mitigate curling and may avoid the development of cracks at the drying surface. Shrinkage measured in the middle region of the semi-cylindrical specimen shows a closer correspondence with macroscopic water loss than shrinkage measured at the surface, as indicated by the alignment between the termination of linear shrinkage in the middle region and the global transition from the CRP to the FRP (Fig.  12 ). This suggests that surface-based measurements tend to overestimate the shrinkage during drying, while shrinkage measured with LVDT at a certain depth more closely reflects the bulk response of the material.

Figure  15  presents the evolution of longitudinal shrinkage as a function of the average gravimetric water content for LMS + IL + Q mixtures (with the same clay content as LMS + IL discussed above but amended with an additional 10 mass-% quartz silt (Q) to increase the workability by having continued granularity, especially when the water content is low) at water-to-solid ratios of 0.14, 0.17, and 0.19. The deformation was measured using an LVDT positioned at the specimen's mid-height. For all mixtures, shrinkage increases progressively as the water content decreases, and the recorded shrinkage clearly reflects the effect of the initial water content, with the mixture having w/s = 0.19 exhibiting the largest shrinkage and the mixture with w/s = 0.14 the smallest. Besides, the w/s 0.17 mixture exhibits a similar trend to that of w/s 0.19, which aligns with the shrinkage behavior when earth materials exceed the liquid limit (with 0.1762 for the LMS + IL + Q mixture here). This similarity indicates that measurements with LVDT provide a simple and reliable method for monitoring the global shrinkage response and facilitate direct comparison of drying behavior between earth materials. Fig. 15 Longitudinal shrinkage as a function of water content of LMS + IL + Q specimens with different water-to-solid contents. Note that the measurements were conducted using the aforementioned setup with semi-cylindrical molds and LVDTs

Attention should be paid to early detection of shrinkage, as earth materials with high water content may initially be too weak to reliably transmit displacement to the LVDTs, leading to incomplete recordings. Although early-stage deformation may be partially missing, it can be approximately estimated using the proportional shrinkage assumption when settlement is known (see Sect. 3.3.1). Moreover, the relevance of shrinkage measurement lies in indicating the cracking risk caused by shrinkage-induced stresses (either due to external restraint or self-restraint). With this perspective, while it is desirable to measure shrinkage as early as possible, the initial shrinkage that cannot activate the LVDT can be generally neglected because it will not induce stress.

sections.heading: Conclusions
paragraphs: This study presented and validated a semi-cylindrical experimental setup for the continuous monitoring of shrinkage in pourable earth materials. By integrating DIC for surface measurements and embedded LVDTs for internal measurements, the deformation of an earth material (with a clay fraction of 15.7 mass-%) with a water-to-solid ratio of 0.1714 and an initial slump of 150 mm was measured from the initial fluid state through the drying process. In addition to shrinkage measurements, surface temperature, mass loss, and capillary pressure were measured and compared with those of a conventional prismatic specimen under identical drying conditions.

Both specimen geometries exhibited similar overall drying kinetics. The rate of mass loss of the specimens remained unchanged during drying for 4–6 h, and it was equal to that of free water, then gradually decreased. During the CRP, the surface temperature remained constant. However, the semi-cylindrical specimen exhibited a shorter CRP, due to its higher surface-to-volume ratio. Regarding the suction (capillary pressure), the semi-cylindrical specimen shows a faster evolution over drying time but a more uniform moisture distribution along the shallower region. The bottom region shows a slower evolution than the prismatic specimen. Notably, the rate of mass loss remained constant for a substantial period after the air entry point.

The shrinkage behaviors measured on two specimens show a similar trend but with different final values and transition times. The measured shrinkage, either vertically or horizontally, on the semi-cylindrical specimen on the surface, is higher than that of the prismatic specimen. Shrinkage initially increased linearly with water loss, then transitioned to a slower rate once the capillary pressure in the bottom region approached the air entry point. As such, the semi-cylindrical specimen experiences greater shrinkage than the prismatic specimen, which desaturates later in the bottom region. Moreover, independent of the geometries, shrinkage in the CRP correlated well with the volume of evaporated water, whereas shrinkage in the FRP followed the Biot-Bishop theory.

Shrinkage within the semi-cylindrical specimen remained heterogeneous, with greater deformation occurring at the surface than in the interior. However, shrinkage measurements by LVDT in the middle region of the specimen reflect better the bulk shrinkage response of the whole specimen than surface measurements. When the convenience of measuring shrinkage with LVDTs (compared to DIC) is also taken into account, the measurement technique developed in this paper shows all its practical advantages for comparing volume changes of different earth mixtures. However, in real-world earth elements, different geometries will be encountered. Earthen walls and panels will in general exhibit complicated shrinkage and cracking behaviors due to their sizes, environmental conditions, and specimen restraints. The proposed setup allows measuring shrinkage in unrestrained conditions, enables robust comparisons between mixtures and shrinkage-reducing additives, and elucidates the underlying mechanisms driving moisture loss and volume changes.
